Only after the wake word is detected does the device begin recording a short clip to send to the cloud. A light on the device usually indicates this active recording state. Can they work without an internet connection? Their core functionality is severely limited without an internet connection. Basic tasks handled on the device, like timers on some models, may work, but any command requiring information lookup, music streaming, or cloud-based processing will fail. Controlling smart home devices via local protocols like Matter or Thread may still work if both the speaker and the device support local execution. How do they tell different voices apart? passages.text: Quick answer Smart speakers work by constantly listening for a wake word, sending your audio command to the cloud for processing by powerful AI, and then executing the response, which could be playing music, answering a question, or controlling a connected smart home device. When you ask your smart speaker to play a song or turn off the lights, you’re triggering a complex, multi-stage technological process that happens in seconds. Understanding how do smart speakers work—from the microphone to the cloud and back—helps you use them more effectively and make informed choices about privacy and compatibility within your smart home setup. Stage 1: The Always-Listening Microphone and Wake Word The journey of a voice command begins with the speaker’s microphone array. These devices are designed to be in a low-power, always-listening state, but they aren’t recording or sending everything they hear to the internet. Instead, a small, dedicated chip on the device runs a simple audio pattern recognition algorithm, doing nothing but listening for its specific wake word, like “Alexa,” “Hey Google,” or “Hey Siri.” This processing happens locally on the device.
